problemText: A dot plot shows data on a number line where each value in a data set gets its own dot. What happens when the same value appears more than once in the data set?
choices: The dots are stacked directly on top of each other above that value.
The dots are placed side by side horizontally next to each other.
Only one dot is drawn, no matter how many times the value appears.
The value is combined with nearby values and shown as a single mark.
hints: Think about what happens to multiple pets at the same number on Ms. Rivera's plot.
The key word is 'stack'—dots are placed vertically, not horizontally.

problemText: A teacher collects data on the number of books read by 8 students: 2, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3, 2, 4. If this data is displayed as a dot plot, how many dots would be stacked above the value 2?
choices: 2 dots
3 dots
4 dots
8 dots
hints: Count how many times the value 2 appears in the list.
Remember that each occurrence of 2 gets its own dot, stacked above that value.

problemText: A histogram displays data with intervals that are all the same width. Why do the bars in a histogram sit directly next to each other with no gaps between them?
choices: Because gaps would make the histogram look cluttered and interrupt the visual flow showing how data is distributed across intervals.
Because histograms must follow a formatting rule that distinguishes them from other graph types used in mathematics and statistics.
Because each value belongs to exactly one interval, and the bars represent consecutive, non-overlapping intervals.
Because the number line must be completely filled to show all possible values without leaving any empty space.
hints: Think about what happens if two intervals overlap or if there is a gap between them.
Every single data value needs to fit into exactly one interval—no value can be counted twice or left out.

problemText: A coach collects data from 25 players on how many goals they scored. The values range from 3 goals all the way to 48 goals, and most players scored a different number. The coach wants to display this data on a single page that is easy to read. Should the coach use a dot plot or a histogram, and what is the main reason?
choices: A dot plot, because it can display any amount of data and makes every individual score visible so nothing gets hidden in intervals.
A histogram, because histograms are more professional and work for any data set no matter the size.
A dot plot, because 25 values is a small data set and small data sets always use dot plots.
A histogram, because there are many values spread across a wide range, and grouping them into intervals keeps the display readable.
hints: Look at the size of the data set (25) and how spread out the values are (3 to 48).
Compare this situation to Mr. Okafor's 20 homework-minutes data—what made a histogram a good choice there?

problemText: A histogram shows how many hours 16 students spent studying for a test. The intervals are 0-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-11 hours. The bars have heights of 4, 6, 4, and 2 respectively. A student looks at the bar above the 6-8 interval and says, 'This bar tells me that 4 students studied for exactly 7 hours.' Why is this statement incorrect?
choices: Because the bar only tells us that 4 students studied somewhere between 6 and 8 hours, not that all of them studied exactly 7 hours.
Because the interval 6-8 contains more than 4 specific values that could be scored, so grouping them loses information about which exact values actually occurred.
Because histograms record frequencies in ranges rather than exact measurements, and 4 students somewhere in that interval could have studied 6, 6.5, 7, 7.5, or 8 hours separately.
Because the bar height represents a frequency count across an entire interval, not the number of students who chose one particular value within that range.
hints: Think about what is lost when individual values are grouped into an interval.
A histogram groups data together for readability—what exact information is no longer visible once values are grouped?

problemText: A teacher displays student test scores on a histogram with equal intervals: 60-69, 70-79, 80-89, and 90-99. The bar heights are 3, 7, 8, and 2 respectively. The teacher then decides to create a dot plot of the same data. What would be a valid concern about making this switch from a histogram to a dot plot?
choices: A dot plot cannot show scores in the 60-69 range because those are too low to measure accurately.
The dot plot would need 20 dots spread across 40 possible exact values, and if students actually scored many different exact scores, the plot could become crowded and hard to read.
A dot plot is not allowed if there are more than 15 data points because the display rules require switching to intervals for larger data sets.
A dot plot would require intervals like the histogram uses, so it would not actually simplify or improve the way the data is shown to viewers.
hints: Count the total number of data values represented by the histogram bars.
Think about how many different exact scores the students could have—if spread across a wide range with many different values, what happens to readability on a dot plot?

problemText: A data set contains these values: 10, 12, 15, 18, 20. What is the mean of this data set?
hints: Add all five values together.
Then divide your sum by how many values there are.

problemText: Four students recorded the number of books they read last month: 3, 5, 7, 9. What is the median number of books read?
hints: The values are already in order, so you do not need to rearrange them.
With an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values.

problemText: Five friends compared how many video games they own: 8, 10, 12, 14, 16. Which statement is true about the mean and median of this data set?
choices: The mean is 12 but the median is 10.
The mean is higher than the median.
The median is higher than the mean.
The mean and median are both 12.
hints: Find the mean by adding all five values and dividing by 5.
Find the median by identifying the middle value when the data is in order.

problemText: A runner recorded her mile times for seven practice runs, in minutes: 6.5, 6.8, 6.9, 7.0, 7.1, 7.2, 12.5. The last time was interrupted by a stop sign, making it much higher than her other runs. Which statement best explains why the median is a better measure of her typical mile time than the mean?
choices: The 12.5 minute run is an outlier that pulls the mean higher, but the median is only affected by the order of values, not by how extreme they are.

The median is computed by finding the middle position in an ordered list, so extreme values like 12.5 do not influence which number sits in the center the way they push the sum higher in the mean calculation.
The mean depends on adding all values together and dividing, so a single very large number like 12.5 affects the mean much more than it affects the median, which depends only on position.
The median always ignores the largest and smallest values in a dataset to focus on the middle range, whereas the mean treats every value equally regardless of how far it sits from the others.
hints: Think about what happens to the mean when one very large value is added to the sum.
Think about what the median cares about — is it the actual size of each value, or something else?

problemText: A teacher records attendance across eight class periods: 28, 29, 29, 30, 30, 31, 31, 32 students present. Calculate both the mean and the median attendance. Then decide which one better describes a typical class size, and explain why.
choices: Mean is 30, median is 30; the mean is always better at describing typical values.
Mean is 30, median is 30; either measure works well because there is no outlier pulling the data apart.
Mean is 30.25, median is 30; the median is better because it ignores the highest and lowest values.
Mean is 30.25, median is 30.5; the mean is more useful because it is larger.
hints: Add all eight values and divide by 8 to find the mean.
The two middle values (4th and 5th) average to find the median; then check whether the data is spread evenly or pulled by an outlier.

problemText: Six friends compared their test scores: 72, 75, 78, 81, 84, 91. The student who scored 91 studied harder than the others. Another student is worried that this high score will make the class average (mean) too high and not represent where most students actually performed. Is this student's concern correct? Justify your answer by calculating both the mean and the median and comparing them to the rest of the data.
choices: Yes, the concern is correct; the 91 pulls the mean up to 80.2 while the median stays at 79.5, so the mean no longer describes the typical student.
Yes, the concern is correct; whenever one score is noticeably higher than all the others, it must be an outlier that forces the mean to be unrepresentative of most students' actual performance.
No, the concern is incorrect; the mean is 80.2 and the median is 79.5, which are both close to most of the scores because 91 is not extreme enough to be an outlier here.
No, the concern is incorrect; the median is 81, which is higher than the mean of 80.2, so the high score pulls the median up more than the mean and actually makes the mean more reliable.
hints: Calculate the mean by adding all six scores and dividing by 6; calculate the median by finding the mean of the 3rd and 4th values when ordered.
An outlier must be far enough from the rest of the data to pull the mean noticeably away — look at whether 91 sits far from the other five scores or reasonably close.

problemText: A data set has a minimum value of 8 and a maximum value of 35. What is the range?
hints: Range is found by subtracting the smallest value from the largest value.
You need to subtract, not add or divide the two numbers.

problemText: A teacher recorded the number of books read by students in one month: 3, 7, 5, 9, 6. After ordering this data from least to greatest, what is the median?
hints: The median is the middle value when the data is ordered from least to greatest.
With 5 values, count to find which one is in the very center position.

problemText: Five friends timed how long they could hold a plank in seconds: 25, 18, 42, 30, 35. The five-number summary for this data is: minimum 18, Q1 = 23.5, median = 30, Q3 = 38.5, maximum = 42. What is the interquartile range (IQR)?
choices: 15 seconds
24 seconds
8.5 seconds
19.5 seconds
hints: The IQR equals Q3 minus Q1.
Subtract the first quartile value from the third quartile value.

problemText: A coach recorded sprint times in seconds for eight runners: 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 19, 21, 25. Order the data, find Q1 and Q3 (remember to leave out the median when splitting an even-count data set), then calculate the range and IQR. Which statement is true?
choices: The range is 13 seconds and the IQR is 4.5 seconds.
The range is 13 seconds and the IQR is 6 seconds.
The range is 10 seconds and the IQR is 6 seconds.
The range is 13 seconds and the IQR is 8.5 seconds.
hints: With 8 values (even), after ordering, the median falls between the two middle values. Split the lower half (first 4 values) and upper half (last 4 values) to find Q1 and Q3.
Range = max − min. IQR = Q3 − Q1. Double-check your Q1 and Q3 by finding the median of each half.

problemText: Two classes took a spelling test. Class A's five-number summary is: min 60, Q1 = 70, median = 80, Q3 = 85, max = 95. Class B's five-number summary is: min 70, Q1 = 75, median = 80, Q3 = 82, max = 90. Both classes have the same median, but which statement correctly uses spread to compare them?
choices: Class A and Class B have identical spread because they share the same median of 80.
Class B has a tighter middle half because the IQRs are both the same value.
Class A has greater spread because its range of 35 is larger than Class B's range of 20.
Class A must have performed better on the test because its maximum score is higher.
hints: A center number alone can hide the story. Compare the ranges and IQRs of both classes, not just their medians.
Calculate: Class A's range and IQR; Class B's range and IQR. Which class shows wider spread in these measures?

problemText: An outdoor club recorded the distance (in meters) each member could throw a ball: 15, 18, 22, 24, 26, 28, 31, 35, 38, 45. After finding the five-number summary and calculating the IQR, one member threw a ball 62 meters on a second attempt—far farther than anyone else. If this 62-meter throw is added to the original data set, which values in the five-number summary would change, and by how much would the IQR change?
choices: Only the maximum would change; the IQR would change by about 7 meters.
The maximum, Q3, median, and IQR would all change significantly.
The median and maximum would both change; the IQR would change by about 2 meters.
Only the maximum would change; the IQR would not change.
hints: The IQR measures only the middle half of the data (from Q1 to Q3). A value far outside that range affects the whiskers but not the box itself.
When you add one new extreme value to a data set, think about which parts of the five-number summary it can actually touch.

problemText: A statistical question is one that anticipates variability in the answers. Which of the following best describes what variability means in this context?
choices: The question asks about information that stays the same when collected from different sources, such as a fact that would be the same in every reference book or online database.
The question requires surveying a large group of people and counting them up to produce one final total number for comparison.
The question uses certain action words like 'how many' or 'how much' rather than request words like 'what' or 'which' in its phrasing.
The answers to the question are expected to differ from one person to another, object to object, or time to time.
hints: Think about what happens when you collect answers from different members of a group. Do the answers stay the same or do they differ?
Variability is about expecting different answers before you ever collect the data.

problemText: A student is deciding between two questions. Question 1: 'How many minutes did it take the school bus to arrive at school this morning?' Question 2: 'How many minutes did it take the school bus to arrive at school on each of the last ten school days?' Use the variability test to identify which one is a statistical question.
choices: Question 2 is a statistical question because different days may have different travel times.
Question 1 is a statistical question because it is asking about the school bus.
Neither question is a statistical question because they both are about the same bus.
Both questions are statistical questions because they both ask about time measurements.
hints: Ask yourself: for Question 1, how many different answers would you expect to collect? For Question 2, how many different answers would you expect?
One bus ride on one morning gives one time, but ten different days could have ten different times due to traffic, weather, or other changes.

problemText: A teacher wants to know about the reading habits of the fifth graders in the school. The teacher is trying to decide which question to ask. Read the two options carefully and decide which one is a statistical question.
choices: How many pages did the fifth-grade class read in total last week?
How many pages did each student in the fifth grade read last week?
How many fifth graders attend this school?
What was the title of the book that the fifth-grade class read together last month?
hints: A statistical question reaches each member of a group separately so that each person can give a different answer.
Even though option A mentions the whole fifth-grade class, it asks for only one total number. That is not the same as asking each student separately.

problemText: Marcus wrote a question: 'How much did the class lunch cost?' He wants to turn this into a statistical question by changing who the question is about. Using the lesson strategy, rewrite Marcus's question so it becomes statistical. Which of the following rewrites correctly applies the variability test?
choices: How much did lunches cost in the school cafeteria over the last year?
What kind of food did the class eat for lunch?
How much did each student in the class spend on lunch today?
How much money does the school spend on food for all student lunches?
hints: To fix Marcus's question, keep the topic (lunch cost) the same and change WHO is being asked—from one event to every member of a group.
Each student is likely to have spent a different amount on lunch, so their answers would vary. The question should ask each student separately.

problemText: A student claims that 'How many students attend Lincoln Middle School?' is a statistical question because it mentions many students. Evaluate this claim using the variability test taught in the lesson.
choices: The claim is correct because asking about a large group of students automatically qualifies as a statistical question by definition, since mentioning multiple people makes any question statistical in nature.
The claim is correct because any question that refers to multiple people or objects in a school setting is considered a statistical question, regardless of what answer the question produces.

The claim is incorrect because the definition of a statistical question requires that different people can give different answers, but asking about total enrollment yields only one fixed number with no variability.
The claim is incorrect because even though the question mentions many students, it produces only one answer: the total enrollment number, and no variability is expected.
hints: Remember: mentioning a group is not enough by itself to make a question statistical. What matters is whether each member of the group can give a separate, different answer.
The school's total enrollment is one fixed number. There is only one correct answer to this question, so no variability is expected.

problemText: A coach wrote three questions to learn about her soccer team: (1) 'What is the height of our team captain?' (2) 'How tall is each player on our team?' (3) 'What was the total combined height of our team members?' For each question, the coach should apply the variability test. How many of these three questions are statistical questions that would produce variability in the answers collected?
choices: Only Question 2 is statistical because different players have different heights and can give separate answers.
All three questions are statistical because they all mention the soccer team and involve measurement.
Questions 1 and 2 are statistical, but Question 3 is not, because Question 3 asks for a single combined total rather than separate responses.
Only Questions 2 and 3 are statistical because they both reference multiple team members rather than singling out one individual.
hints: Apply the variability test to each one: does it ask one specific person or object (one answer), or does it ask each member of a group separately (many possibly different answers)?
Question 1 names one specific person so it has one answer. Question 3 asks for one total number for the whole group. Only Question 2 asks each player separately.
